The rising volatility and increasing strategic importance of the Arctic has long been acknowledged, but in 2024, competition in the region became even more pitched. On 24 July, the North American Aerospace Defense Command intercepted a Russian and a Chinese military aircraft operating in the Alaska air defense identification zone in the Arctic. In early October, two Russian Border Guard ships and two Chinese Coast Guard ships conducted a joint maritime patrol approximately 440 miles southwest of St. Lawrence Island in the Bering Sea.
These first-ever joint Russian and Chinese deployments show how far the geopolitical dynamics in the Arctic region have already shifted and why the U.S. must respond decisively

Challenges posed by Russia and China

Over the past decade, Russia has reestablished 14 Cold War–era Arctic military bases and launched icebreaking warships. It held a massive naval exercise in the Bering Sea that displaced American fishing vessels working in the U.S. exclusive economic zone and continued its posturing through military exercises that have included antiship cruise missiles fired from submarines.

Russia has never stopped making expansive and unsupported claims on Arctic resources. A Russian politician recently floated the idea of seizing Alaska as retaliation for U.S. sanctions. The conflict in Ukraine shows Russia’s ability to commit to a losing cause, almost certainly because the country Russia is invading, in that case, is deeply engrained in Putin’s sense of Russian national identity. The Arctic would almost certainly fall into the same broad category.

For its part, China in 2020 launched its first domestically built icebreaker and recently announced intentions to build a nuclear-powered icebreaker. As China and Russia continue to explore the depths of their “friendship without limits,” their collaboration in the Arctic domain is inevitable and only heightens the threat to U.S. interests.

The strategic importance of the Arctic is not news. However, many Americans have not been informed on how a failure to invest in this overlooked and misunderstood part of the world could have dire and lasting consequences for national security. The State Department recognized the Arctic’s growing strategic importance when it nominated Michael Sfraga as the first-ever ambassador at large for the Arctic region. DoD did the same when it established the Ted Stevens Center for Arctic Security Studies and the office of Arctic and Global Resilience Office at the Pentagon, led by a new a Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense. The first deputy assistant secretary who served in this position, Iris Ferguson, summed up the problem succinctly: “There might not be conflict now—and there hopefully will never be conflict in the Arctic—but we need to be prepared to operate there.”
Threats from major strategic competitors are not the only challenges facing the United States and its allies in the Arctic.

Global distant-water fishing fleets—especially those led by China and defended by the China Coast Guard—will not be far behind. Despite the United States’ December 2023 claim for an Extended Continental Shelf—a provision granted by Article 76 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea—the looming rush for resources will test U.S. regulations and the country’s ability to defend its sovereign rights to those resources.

Within DoD, the Arctic straddles the seams between Northern Command (NorthCom), Indo-Pacific Command (IndoPaCom), and European Command (EuCom) in the President’s Unified Command Plan. The region’s vast range, austere and remote operating environment, and unique mission profiles demanding specialized capabilities all inform the governance model needed to manage it. Compounding this complexity is the prudent, and in some instances legally required, consideration of indigenous, international, interagency, industry, and scientific (4IS) needs prior to engaging in any Arctic-focused operation, activity, or investment.

In fall 2023, the Coast Guard tacitly acknowledged C2 seams between the east and west Arctic and the strictly domestic focus of the District 17 (Alaska) Commander. They launched a proof-of-concept effort to enhance and unify C2 for its operations in the Arctic by establishing Coast Guard Task Force (CGTF) Arctic. The Coast Guard Pacific Area Deputy Commander, a two-star rear admiral, has been designated to serve as the task force’s first commander. When tasked and allocated with resources, CGTF Arctic plans, synchronizes, and exercises tactical control of Coast Guard forces for missions in the Arctic. This Arctic task force concept should be expanded by including allied, joint-force, and whole-of-government capacities. That should be the structure for the ACITF.

. The interagency task-force model has been used with great success by Joint Interagency Task Force (JIATF) South and JIATF West. It provides all stakeholders a forum to identify threats, fuse actionable intelligence into operational tasking, project hard or soft/smart power to provide influential presence, and mount an active defense to counter threats. In addition, the United States already has arrived at this solution for the other end of the Earth, with the long-standing operation of Joint Task Force–Support Forces Antarctica, working for U.S. Air Force Pacific and IndoPaCom.

. Several actions would set up the proposed ACITF establishment for success:

1) The mission must be statutorily defined, and the President’s Unified Command Plan must be updated to reflect the task force’s roles, responsibilities, and authorities to interface with the applicable DoD Geographic Combatant Commands within the Arctic region.

2) As an emerging requirement, this organization will likely demand new resources. Until such resources can be allocated, the responsibilities, efficiency, and function of other DoD joint, combined, and interagency task forces would be a prudent place to harvest resources to stand up the ACITF. The mission performance metrics and personnel and funding allocations must build on the lessons learned from many previous Joint and Combined Task Forces.

3) The military threat demands an organization that heeds the tenets of Joint Publication 1, as well as other applicable allied and interagency joint publications. This task force would depend on intergovernmental and international interoperability to succeed. That is why the ACITF must be a DoD initiative with integral support from the U.S. Coast Guard and the Department of State.

As with JIATF South and JIATF West, heading the organization with a Coast Guard flag officer makes sense. This would acknowledge the Coast Guard’s role as lead federal agency for Arctic operations and leverage the Coast Guard’s Title 10 and Title 14 authorities and missions.
